title: The Superorganism
description: How many ants there are, why a colony can behave like one body, and where ants came from

concepts.title: Twenty Quadrillion Ants
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2022 a team of ecologists led by Patrick Schultheiss and Sabine Nooten tried to count the world's ants. They pooled 489 field studies from every continent where ants live, mostly counts from leaf litter and the ground surface made with pitfall traps and litter samples, then scaled the densities up habitat by habitat. Their answer, published in PNAS, was about 20 quadrillion ants: 20 followed by 15 zeros, or roughly 2.5 million for every person alive.

Measured as dry carbon, those ants come to about 12 megatons. That is more than all wild birds and wild mammals combined, and about a fifth of the carbon in human bodies. The result corrects a popular claim, repeated for decades, that the world's ants weigh about as much as its people. Densities were highest in the tropics.

The figure is a floor, not a census, and the authors called it conservative. Ants living in tree canopies or deep underground were poorly sampled, and large parts of Africa and Asia had few studies. Earlier numbers, such as the one to ten quadrillion that E. O. Wilson often cited, were extrapolations from rough estimates of insect numbers in general. About 14,000 ant species have been named so far, and specialists expect thousands more to be described.

concepts.title: The Colony as an Organism
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1911 the Harvard entomologist William Morton Wheeler published an essay with a provocative title, "The Ant-Colony as an Organism." He argued that a colony passes the tests biologists use for an individual animal: it behaves as a unit, has its own peculiarities of behavior, size and structure, goes through a cycle of growth, and reproduces by sending out winged queens and males. Wheeler compared the queen and males to an organism's reproductive cells and the sterile workers to its body, which feeds, builds and defends, then dies without offspring. He and later writers used the word superorganism for such a colony.

The idea fell out of favor in the mid-twentieth century. Biologists such as George C. Williams and W. D. Hamilton taught the field to explain behavior by its effects on genes and individuals, and talk of a colony's own goals began to sound mystical. On the new view, a colony looked less like a body than like an alliance of relatives whose interests mostly, but not always, coincide.

The superorganism came back in the late 1980s, in papers such as David Sloan Wilson and Elliott Sober's "Reviving the Superorganism" (1989), and in Bert Hölldobler and E. O. Wilson's book The Superorganism (2008). Most myrmecologists now treat it as a matter of degree. A colony of a few dozen workers, each still able to lay eggs, is a loose society. A leafcutter colony with millions of workers, castes of very different body sizes and one queen laying eggs for up to 15 years behaves much more like a single body.

concepts.title: Wasps That Went Social
concepts.contentHtml:
Ants are wasps that took to the ground and to colony life. A 2013 genomic study placed them closest to the bees and their wasp relatives, the Apoidea, rather than to the hornets they superficially resemble. The oldest known ant fossil, Vulcanidris cratensis, was described in 2025 from limestone of the Crato Formation in Brazil, about 113 million years old. It belongs to the extinct hell ants, whose jaws swung upward instead of closing sideways like those of living ants. Molecular dating puts the first ants somewhat earlier still.

For most of the Cretaceous, ants were rare, about 1 percent of the insects found in fossils of that era. By the Oligocene and Miocene they made up 20 to 40 percent of insects in major fossil deposits, a rise that tracked the spread of flowering plants and the forests and leaf litter they created.

Why would workers give up reproducing? Hamilton's 1964 answer leaned on haplodiploidy: male ants hatch from unfertilized eggs, so sisters with the same father share three-quarters of their genes, more than the half they would share with daughters. That argument has weakened. Termites are fully diploid yet social, and many ant queens mate with several males, which lowers relatedness among workers. A 2008 study of 267 bee, wasp and ant species found that single mating was ancestral in all eight social lineages examined, which keeps kinship central. In 2010 Martin Nowak, Corina Tarnita and E. O. Wilson argued in Nature that kin selection was unnecessary to explain social insects; more than 130 researchers signed a reply defending it. Most specialists still side with kin selection.

title: Decisions Without Leaders
description: How trails, quorums and chance encounters let colonies choose with nobody in charge

concepts.title: The Double Bridge
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1989 Simon Goss, Jean-Louis Deneubourg and colleagues in Brussels connected a nest of Argentine ants to food by a bridge with two branches, one much longer than the other. Most traffic soon ran over the short branch, although no ant had measured anything. Ants that happened to take the short route reached the food and returned sooner, laying trail pheromone as they went, so the short branch gained scent faster, drew more ants and gained more scent still. In a related experiment with two equal branches, colonies still settled on one, picked by chance early differences in traffic.

This is positive feedback, and many ant species organize foraging with it. The French biologist Pierre-Paul Grassé coined a word for this kind of coordination in 1959, while studying termite nest building: stigmergy, in which individuals respond to marks others have left in the environment rather than to each other directly. A pheromone trail is a stigmergic message, written on the ground and read by whoever passes.

The bridge also exposed a weakness. When the short branch was added only after a trail on the long one had formed, most ants kept using the long route, because real pheromone fades too slowly to erase a habit. In his 1992 doctoral thesis in Milan, Marco Dorigo turned the experiment into an algorithm, ant colony optimization. Virtual ants wander a network of possible routes and deposit virtual pheromone in proportion to the quality of the solution they found, and the deposits evaporate each round. Evaporation much faster than in nature keeps the search from locking onto an early, mediocre answer. The first version tackled the traveling salesman problem.

concepts.title: House Hunting by Quorum
concepts.contentHtml:
The rock ant Temnothorax albipennis lives in colonies of at most a few hundred workers, packed into a single crack in a rock. In Nigel Franks's laboratory at the University of Bristol, colonies live in nests made from two microscope slides, and when researchers remove the roof, the colony must find a new home quickly. Scouts fan out and inspect candidate cavities, judging floor area, ceiling height, darkness and the width of the entrance.

A scout that likes a site recruits by tandem running: she leads a single follower, which keeps tapping her with its antennae, from the old nest to the new one. The better the site, the sooner scouts start recruiting, so good sites gather ants faster. Each ant also senses how crowded a new site is. Once the number there passes a threshold, a quorum, recruiters switch from slow tandem runs to picking up nestmates, brood and queen and carrying them, which is much faster. The colony has decided, though no single ant compared the options. Experiments show colonies choose the better of two sites even when most scouts have visited only one.

The quorum can shift. Under harsh conditions colonies use lower thresholds, deciding faster but making more mistakes, a classic trade-off between speed and accuracy. In 2006 Franks and Tom Richardson argued in Nature that tandem running counts as teaching, because leaders slow down for followers that lag, at a cost to themselves. Critics replied that it may not meet stricter definitions of teaching, and the label is still argued over. Honeybee swarms, studied by Thomas Seeley, choose new homes with a strikingly similar quorum rule.

concepts.title: The Queen Is Not in Charge
concepts.contentHtml:
The word "queen" misleads. An ant queen lays eggs; she does not give orders, and in many species a colony has dozens or hundreds of queens. No ant knows how many foragers the colony needs, how much food is stored, or where the nest needs repair. Work gets allocated anyway, through local cues each ant can sense.

Deborah Gordon of Stanford University has followed colonies of the red harvester ant, Pogonomyrmex barbatus, in the desert of the American Southwest since the 1980s. A colony lives as long as its single queen, two decades or more. Gordon found that foragers decide whether to go out based on how often they meet ants returning with seeds. Quick returns mean food is plentiful, so more foragers leave; on hot, dry days with slow returns, foragers stay in and save water. In 2012 Gordon and the Stanford engineer Balaji Prabhakar pointed out that this resembles how the internet's TCP protocol paces data by the rate of acknowledgments coming back, and the press dubbed it the "anternet."

Division of labor also follows age. Young workers stay deep inside tending brood; older ones take the risky jobs outside, so the colony spends the members with the least life left on the most dangerous work. Not every worker is busy. Studies of Temnothorax in Anna Dornhaus's laboratory at the University of Arizona found that a large share of workers sits idle much of the time, in the wild as well as in the lab. When researchers removed the most active workers, formerly idle ones took over their jobs, which suggests the idlers serve partly as a reserve.

title: Farmers and Herders
description: Ants that grow fungus, keep insect herds and turn their own bodies into storage jars

concepts.title: The Leafcutters' Gardens
concepts.contentHtml:
A column of leafcutter ants crossing a forest path carries green fragments bigger than the carriers, but the ants do not eat leaves. Inside the nest, smaller workers lick the pieces clean, chew them into pulp, manure the pulp with their own fecal droplets and plant it with tufts of fungus. The crop is Leucoagaricus gongylophorus, a fungus that depends entirely on the ants. It produces swollen, nutrient-rich hyphal tips called gongylidia, which the ants, and above all their larvae, eat. The leafcutters, chiefly the genera Atta and Acromyrmex, range from the southern United States to Argentina.

A mature Atta colony holds millions of workers in castes of very different sizes. The smallest tend the fungus and brood; medium workers cut and carry; big-headed soldiers defend the nest. Tiny workers often ride on the cut leaves, guarding the carriers from parasitic phorid flies. Waste is a separate job: a dedicated crew hauls spent fungus and dead ants to refuse dumps, away from the garden. Leafcutters strip so much vegetation that they are often called the dominant herbivores of the American tropics.

Each garden starts with a theft from home. A young queen leaves on her mating flight with a pellet of fungus from her mother's garden tucked into a pouch in her mouth, the infrabuccal pocket. After mating and shedding her wings she digs a chamber, spits out the pellet and tends the new garden herself, fertilizing it with her own feces, until her first workers take over. An Atta queen can live up to about 15 years.

concepts.title: Sixty-Six Million Years of Farming
concepts.contentHtml:
Leafcutters are the newest branch of a lineage of about 250 fungus-farming ant species, all in the Americas. Most farm on a smaller scale, feeding their gardens dead leaves, insect droppings and other debris rather than fresh leaves. A 2024 genomic study in Science led by Ted Schultz of the Smithsonian dated the origin of ant agriculture to about 66 million years ago, close to the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs. The authors suggest that in the dim, plant-starved aftermath, fungi feeding on decay flourished and some ants came to rely on them. Older estimates put the origin at 55 to 60 million years ago. Either way, ants were farming tens of millions of years before humans began, about 12,000 years ago.

Later came "higher agriculture," in which the fungi became fully domesticated and can no longer live on their own, and later still leafcutting, within roughly the last 20 million years. Like human farmers, the ants grow essentially one crop strain in each nest, and monocultures invite disease. The gardens' chief pest is Escovopsis, a fungus that attacks the ants' cultivated fungus.

In 1999 Cameron Currie and colleagues reported in Nature that the ants fight Escovopsis with another partner: filamentous bacteria growing on their bodies that secrete antibiotics. Later work identified these mostly as Pseudonocardia. Workers also weed, cutting out infected patches and carrying them away, and they secrete antimicrobial compounds from their own glands. How much each defense matters, and whether the bacteria are as central as first thought, is still debated.

concepts.title: Dairy Herds and Living Larders
concepts.contentHtml:
Many ants keep livestock. Aphids, scale insects and mealybugs suck plant sap and excrete the surplus sugar as honeydew. Ants such as the black garden ant, Lasius niger, stroke aphids with their antennae to collect the droplets and drive away ladybird beetles and other predators. Some species store aphid eggs in their nests over winter and carry the hatchlings back to plants in spring, and the yellow meadow ant, Lasius flavus, keeps herds of root-feeding aphids underground. The relationship is not purely friendly: ants also kill and eat some of the aphids they tend.

The most committed herders belong to the genus Acropyga, which live underground with root-feeding mealybugs. A young queen leaves on her mating flight carrying a pregnant mealybug in her jaws, seeding the herd of her future colony. Ants preserved doing exactly this in Dominican amber show the partnership is about 20 million years old.

Other ants store food inside their own bodies. In honeypot ants, certain workers called repletes are fed nectar and honeydew until their abdomens swell, in the North American desert species Myrmecocystus mexicanus to the size of grapes. They hang from the ceilings of underground chambers and give food back to nestmates in lean times. In one colony of the Australian Camponotus inflatus, 49 percent of 1,063 ants were repletes. Aboriginal Australians dig as deep as two meters to reach them, and the Tjupan people have used the honey for sore throats, colds and skin infections; laboratory tests have found it has antimicrobial activity.

title: Pirates and Puppeteers
description: Ants that steal other ants' young, lodge in other colonies for free, or fall to a body-snatching fungus

concepts.title: Huber's Raiders and Darwin's Doubts
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1810 the Genevan naturalist Pierre Huber described behavior few had suspected in insects. Columns of the reddish ant Polyergus rufescens marched on nests of darker Formica ants, carried off their pupae and reared them at home, where the captives grew up to do nearly all the work. Huber called them "auxiliary ants." The raiders' sickle-shaped jaws are superb weapons and almost useless for anything else. Huber shut 30 raiders in with food and their own brood but no helpers. They did nothing, could not even feed themselves, and many starved. When he added a single Formica worker, she set to work at once, fed the survivors and tended the larvae.

Charles Darwin gave the case several pages in the chapter on instinct in On the Origin of Species (1859). He credited Huber, then checked an English species himself, Formica sanguinea, which keeps captives but can survive without them. He opened 14 nests and found a few captives in every one, and spent many hours watching nests in Surrey and Sussex. On how the habit began, he said he would "not pretend to conjecture," then offered a guess: ants that raided nests for pupae to eat might have let some hatch, and found them useful.

Biologists call the behavior dulosis, from the Greek doulos, slave, and older literature speaks of "slave-making ants." In 2007 the ecologist Joan Herbers argued in BioScience that the metaphor is racially loaded, and proposed "pirate ants"; many researchers now say "social parasites." A new Polyergus queen founds her colony by entering a Formica nest, killing its queen and being adopted by its workers.

concepts.title: Rebels, Lodgers and Emery's Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
In the forests of eastern North America the small ant Temnothorax americanus, long known as Protomognathus americanus, raids colonies of its relative Temnothorax longispinosus. In 2009 Alexandra Achenbach and Susanne Foitzik reported what they called the first evidence of slave rebellion: captive workers systematically killed many of the parasite's developing pupae. The captives gain nothing directly, since they never return home. The likely payoff is indirect: fewer parasites mean fewer raids on nearby nests, which are often headed by the captives' relatives.

Social parasitism has evolved again and again; brood raiding of this kind alone at least ten times. In 1909 the Italian entomologist Carlo Emery noted that social parasites tend to be close relatives of their hosts, a pattern now called Emery's rule. One explanation is that a parasite can arise inside its host species and split off while still living in the same nests. A 2014 genetic study of the Brazilian fungus-farming ant Mycocepurus castrator and its host Mycocepurus goeldii supported that route, a rare case of a new species forming without geographic separation.

The end of this road is the workerless inquiline, a lodger that has given up workers altogether. Teleutomyrmex schneideri (now often classified as Tetramorium inquilinum), described by the Swiss myrmecologist Heinrich Kutter in 1950 from Saas-Fee in the Alps, lives in nests of Tetramorium pavement ants. Its queens, about 2.5 millimeters long, cling to the host queen's body, up to eight at once, and are fed by host workers. They have weak jaws, a thin exoskeleton and a reduced brain and nerve cord. Hölldobler and Wilson called it the "ultimate" parasitic ant.

concepts.title: The Zombie-Ant Fungus
concepts.contentHtml:
In Thai rainforests the carpenter ant Camponotus leonardi lives high in the canopy. When one is infected by the fungus Ophiocordyceps unilateralis, it leaves the colony's trails, descends and clamps its jaws onto a vein on the underside of a leaf, usually about 25 centimeters above the forest floor, where humidity and temperature suit the fungus. Field studies found that the biting clustered around solar noon. The ant dies in that death grip. Later a stalk grows from the back of its head and releases spores onto the ground below, where foragers pass.

How the fungus steers the ant is still being worked out. A 2017 study that reconstructed infected ants in three dimensions found fungal cells forming connected networks through the body and wrapped around muscles, including those that work the jaws, but not inside the brain. That points to a fungus acting on the body and perhaps chemically on behavior, rather than literally taking over the brain, as popular accounts often say. The partnership is old: leaves from Germany's Messel pit, about 48 million years old, carry scars matching the death grip.

Despite its name, O. unilateralis is not one species but a complex of many, each mostly specialized on a particular ant host; a single 2018 paper described 14 new members. Colonies are not defenseless: healthy workers groom one another and carry infected nestmates away from the nest. The fungus inspired the infected humans of the video game The Last of Us and its 2023 television adaptation. That remains fiction: these fungi are tied to particular insect hosts, and none is known to infect mammals.

title: Supercolonies
description: How the Argentine ant built a colony spanning continents, and what other invaders do with the same trick

concepts.title: One Colony, Six Thousand Kilometers
concepts.contentHtml:
Most ants treat any ant from another nest as an enemy. Argentine ants in southern Europe do not. In 2002 Tatiana Giraud, Jes Pedersen and Laurent Keller sampled Argentine ants from 33 sites along about 6,000 kilometers of coast, from Italy along the Mediterranean to the Atlantic coast of the Iberian Peninsula, and staged meetings between workers. Ants from 30 of the sites treated one another as nestmates. They belonged to a single supercolony, which the authors estimated held millions of nests and billions of workers. The other three sites belonged to a second, smaller supercolony in Spain, whose workers fought the main one.

Linepithema humile comes from riverside lowlands of the Paraná River basin, in northern Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and southern Brazil. Carried by human trade, it had crossed oceans by the late nineteenth century and now lives on every continent except Antarctica, mostly where the climate is mild and Mediterranean-like. In California one "Very Large Colony" stretches from San Diego to beyond San Francisco.

In 2009 a team led by Eiriki Sunamura in Japan put together workers from the largest supercolonies of Europe, California and Japan. They did not fight, and behaved as if they belonged to a single colony. These populations exchange no workers or queens across oceans, but they share a chemical identity, probably because they descend from closely related invading stock. Some researchers call the result a global megacolony, the most populous animal society known. Whether it is one colony is partly a matter of definition: the populations share an identity, not a working life.

concepts.title: Why the Borders Disappeared
concepts.contentHtml:
Ants recognize nestmates by smell, chiefly a waxy coat of hydrocarbons on the cuticle whose blend is partly inherited. In their native South America, Argentine ants are genetically more diverse and live in much smaller colonies that fight their neighbors. Introduced populations are far more uniform. In 2000 Neil Tsutsui and colleagues showed that Argentine ants in California had lost much of the species' genetic variation, and that the loss went with reduced aggression: neighbors smelled too much alike to be treated as strangers.

How the uniformity arose is debated. One view stresses a founding bottleneck: the few ants that arrived carried only part of the species' diversity. Another adds selection after arrival, in which colonies with rare recognition cues were attacked by everyone else and lost out, leaving a common identity. Freed from fighting one another, the ants put their effort into foraging and swarming over native ants, which they displace across much of the invaded range.

The borders that remain are violent. In San Diego County the Very Large Colony meets a rival supercolony, the Lake Hodges colony, and a 2006 study documented a front where fighting kills, by one estimate, about 30 million workers a year. Supercolonies also pose an evolutionary puzzle. Workers help nestmates who are barely more related to them than random members of the species, which removes the kinship usually invoked to explain why workers help at all. Some biologists suspect that such populations are an evolutionary dead end, spectacular over centuries but unlikely to last over geological time. That is a prediction, not an observation.

concepts.title: Hokkaido and Christmas Island
concepts.contentHtml:
Argentine ants are not the only ants to erase borders. On the Ishikari coast of Hokkaido in Japan, a survey published in 1979 found that a supercolony of the wood ant Formica yessensis occupied about 45,000 nests connected by underground passages over 2.7 square kilometers, with an estimated 306 million workers and about a million queens. Until the Argentine ant studies, it was the largest supercolony known.

The yellow crazy ant, Anoplolepis gracilipes, shows what a supercolony can do to an island. It reached Christmas Island in the Indian Ocean in the early twentieth century, and supercolonies were first noticed there around 1989. Workers spray formic acid, which can blind the island's famous red land crabs, and the ants have killed millions of them. In 2003 Dennis O'Dowd and colleagues called the result an "invasional meltdown." With crabs gone from parts of the forest floor, seedlings and leaf litter piled up, while the ants tended scale insects in the canopy whose honeydew fed the ants in turn.

Managers fought back with poison baits dropped by helicopter. A 2009 campaign cut ant densities in treated areas by 99 percent, but colonies reinvaded. In 2016 Australian authorities brought in a tiny wasp, Tachardiaephagus somervillei, that attacks the yellow lac scale insect, one of the ants' main sources of honeydew. The idea is to starve the supercolony of sugar by breaking its partnership rather than poisoning the ants directly. Whether it works on an island-wide scale is still being assessed.

title: Armies and Arsenals
description: Army ants that march in circles until they die and build nests from their own bodies, and ants armed with springs and explosives

concepts.title: The Death Spiral
concepts.contentHtml:
In his 1921 book Edge of the Jungle, the naturalist William Beebe described a sight from British Guiana: a column of army ants marching in a circle about 370 meters (roughly 1,200 feet) around, each ant taking about two and a half hours to complete a lap. The ants were going nowhere. Such a circular mill, often called a death spiral, can continue until many of the ants die of exhaustion.

The explanation lies in how army ants travel. Their workers are blind or nearly so, and they move in columns by following the pheromone trail laid by the ants just ahead. If the front of a column loops back onto its own rear, perhaps on open ground with few obstacles to break the loop, each ant keeps faithfully following the one in front. A rule that serves the colony every day becomes a trap. T. C. Schneirla of the American Museum of Natural History, who began studying army ants on Barro Colorado Island in Panama in 1932, analyzed a mill in a 1944 paper and used it to argue that much of army ant movement comes from simple trail following rather than any sense of direction.

Mills have since been reproduced in laboratories and in computer simulations of trail-following agents. They appear to be rare in nature, probably because real terrain is messy: ants at the edges stray, roots and leaves break up the loop, and new raid trails pull ants away. The mill is the price of a system with no leader to notice that the march has become pointless.

concepts.title: Living Nests and Swarm Raids
concepts.contentHtml:
The best-studied army ant, Eciton burchellii of the American tropics, has no permanent nest. A colony of roughly 100,000 to 600,000 workers builds a bivouac out of its own bodies, workers hooking their claws together into a hanging mass that shelters the queen and brood. A swarm raid of up to 200,000 ants fans across the forest floor in a front up to about 20 meters wide, overwhelming insects, spiders and the brood of other ants. Workers plug potholes in the trail with their bodies and link into living bridges across gaps, adjusting both as traffic changes.

Schneirla showed that colonies alternate between two phases. In the statary phase, about three weeks long, the colony stays in one bivouac while the queen lays a huge batch of eggs. In the nomadic phase, about two weeks, it raids daily and moves to a new bivouac almost every night. He argued that the brood drives the cycle: masses of hungry larvae stimulate workers to raid and roam, and when the larvae spin cocoons the colony settles. Army ant queens are wingless, so colonies reproduce by splitting, while winged males, nicknamed sausage flies, fly off to seek other colonies.

A survey led by Carl Rettenmeyer recorded 557 animal species associated with E. burchellii, around 300 of which seem to depend on it, from mites and beetles to antbirds that follow raids and snap up fleeing insects. A 2003 genetic study by Sean Brady concluded that the army ants of the Americas, Africa and Asia share a single origin about 100 million years ago, but a larger 2019 analysis favored separate origins in the Old and New Worlds, so the question is still open.

concepts.title: Exploding, Snapping and Leaping Ants
concepts.contentHtml:
Some ants defend their colonies by self-destruction. Workers of Colobopsis explodens, a relative of carpenter ants from Southeast Asian rainforests including Borneo, respond to an intruder by contracting their abdomens until the body wall bursts, releasing a sticky, bright yellow, spicy-smelling secretion from enlarged mandibular glands. The behavior, called autothysis, was first recorded in 1916 and described in detail in 1974. C. explodens was formally named in 2018 as a model species for studying it. A few termites have evolved comparable suicidal defenses.

Trap-jaw ants of the genus Odontomachus lock their long mandibles open like a cocked spring. When trigger hairs touch prey, the jaws snap shut. In 2006 Sheila Patek and colleagues filmed Odontomachus bauri with high-speed cameras and measured closing speeds of about 35 to 64 meters per second, with a strike lasting on average 0.13 milliseconds. Aimed at the ground, the same strike throws the ant into the air: escape jumps reach about 7 centimeters high, and strikes against an intruder can bounce the ant up to 40 centimeters away.

The record holder uses a different design. The Dracula ant Mystrium camillae presses the tips of its mandibles together until one slips past the other, like a finger snap, with spring, latch and lever combined in the mandible itself. In 2018 Fredrick Larabee and colleagues clocked the snap at up to about 90 meters per second, the fastest animal movement then recorded. The group's nickname comes from adult Dracula ants feeding on the blood-like hemolymph of their own larvae without killing them.
